abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: This study aimed to advance the understanding of factors that predict mean sleep latency (MSL) on the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) by applying machine learning methodology on a high‐dimensional dataset from a large community sample. A cross‐sectional analytic dataset of first visit clinical‐protocol MSLTs (without shift workers) was developed from the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort Study, a community‐based longitudinal study of middle‐aged to older adults in Wisconsin, USA. Fifty predictors captured demographics, medical and psychiatric health, sleep (diary; polysomnography [PSG]) and circadian characteristics. The random forest (RF) algorithm identified the 10 most important predictors, which underwent subsequent regression analyses. Primary analyses focused on MSLT MSL, whereas secondary analyses centred on nap‐specific sleep latencies. Post hoc analyses further explored the relationship between circadian preference and MSLT MSL. The primary sample (n = 301) of middle‐aged adults (mean age = 57.5 ± 7.71 years) was predominantly non‐Hispanic White (97%) and nearly equal across sexes (percentage female = 51.8%). RF model showed low explanatory value for MSLT MSL (R 2 = 12%) with PSG sleep onset latency, circadian preference, daily caffeine use and Epworth Sleepiness Scale emerging as the most important predictors of MSLT MSL in the dataset. Top predictors varied across nap‐specific sleep latency. Morning preference displayed significantly longer MSLT MSL, relative to neither and evening preferences. The low explanatory value observed in our high‐dimensional RF models seemingly reflects the complexity and variability of the MSLT. Additionally, our results underscore the importance and challenge of accounting for circadian characteristics when utilising the MSLT.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) was developed as a ‘measure of physiological sleep tendency in the absence of altering factors’ (Carskadon and Dement 1982). Briefly, the MSLT is an objective test that traditionally consists of four to five daytime naps administered 2‐h apart, with the protocol occurring on the day following an in‐laboratory nighttime polysomnography (PSG) (Krahn et al. 2021). Mean sleep latency (MSL) is computed by averaging the time to fall asleep across napping opportunities, with MSLT MSL ≤ 8 min indicative of clinically significant objective daytime sleepiness. Currently, the MSLT is recognised as the gold standard objective measure of daytime sleepiness (Arand and Bonnet 2019). Notably, the MSLT serves an important role in sleep medicine, acting as a core measure in the diagnostic assessment of central disorders of hypersomnolence, such as narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia (American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2023).

Though recognised as the gold standard measure of daytime sleepiness and serving an important role in sleep medicine, the MSLT protocol is time‐consuming, labour‐intensive and expensive. There is also a growing body of evidence suggesting poor test–retest reliability outside of narcolepsy type 1 (Lopez et al. 2017; Ruoff et al. 2018; Trotti et al. 2013). Furthermore, research has demonstrated weak, inconsistent relationships between MSLT MSL and other objective measures of daytime sleepiness (Krahn et al. 2021; Plante et al. 2020). Additionally, research has suggested that the MSLT is vulnerable to false positives (i.e., MSL ≤ 8 min) in persons who do not have complaints of daytime sleepiness (Harrison and Horne 1996; Johns 2000). Currently, there is poor understanding of what factors predict MSLT MSL, a gap in knowledge that potentially contributes to these shortcomings of the MSLT. Better understanding the predictive factors of MSLT MSL may be useful for guiding the evolution of the MSLT while also potentially advancing the knowledge of daytime sleepiness more generally. Furthermore, clarifying factors that principally influence the MSLT is useful for informing best practice clinical guidelines (Krahn et al. 2021) while also aiding physicians in their diagnostic decision making when interpreting MSLT results.

Across the existing literature related to predictive factors of MSLT MSL, demographics (e.g., age and sex) (Cairns et al. 2018), habitual sleep characteristics preceding the MSLT (e.g., nightly duration) (Kelly et al. 2022), PSG variables collected on the night prior to MSLT (e.g., sleep onset latency [SOL], total sleep time and apnea‐hypopnea index [AHI]) (Chervin et al. 1995; Goldbart et al. 2014; Iskander et al. 2023; Kayumov et al. 2000), circadian characteristics (e.g., timing of dim light melatonin onset and circadian preference [CP]) (Carskadon et al. 1998; Rosenthal et al. 2001), psychiatric conditions (e.g., depression) (Plante et al. 2016), other individual characteristics (e.g., shift worker status) (Goldbart et al. 2014), medication (Kolla et al. 2020), caffeine (Drake et al. 2003) and alcohol (Drake et al. 2003) use have been associated with MSLT MSL. However, there are limitations of the existing research literature. Most of the research has been conducted using samples that are limited in size, as well as the number and scope of predictors (Carskadon et al. 1998; Kayumov et al. 2000; Rosenthal et al. 2001). Additionally, previously employed analytical approaches have limited the ability to evaluate relationships in high‐dimensional data. Most of the previous research has assessed relationships between predictors and MSLT MSL using univariate analyses or with techniques that only account for a small number of factors (Chervin et al. 1995; Goldbart et al. 2014). This has hindered an accurate understanding of the most important predictors for MSLT MSL. Machine learning techniques, such as random forest (RF) (Fernández‐Delgado et al. 2014; Sarker 2021), can handle a large number of variables simultaneously while also benefiting from an ensemble approach that averages results from numerous analyses to enhance accuracy. These techniques are also less susceptible to bias from multicollinearity among predictors, relative to traditional statistical methods (Lindner et al. 2022). Moreover, traditional statistical methods often assume linear relationships, whereas machine learning techniques have the potential to capture non‐linear, more complex patterns (Sarker 2021). The advantages of machine learning techniques often lead to increased predictive performance, which has the potential to provide a more comprehensive and reliable understanding of the most important factors influencing MSLT MSL.

We designed this investigation to advance the understanding of the MSLT by applying machine learning methodology in a large, community‐based sample across a predictor dataset that included demographic, medical and psychiatric, habitual sleep, PSG sleep and circadian characteristics associated with sleepiness. Our primary aim was to identify the most important predictors of MSLT MSL in our dataset, with secondary analyses performed to identify top nap‐specific predictors of sleep latency. We first utilised RF (Fernández‐Delgado et al. 2014) to identify important predictors of the MSLT and followed with regression analyses to further evaluate the relationships of these predictors with MSLT MSL and nap‐specific sleep latency. Post hoc analyses explored the influence of CP on MSLT MSL.

sec.title: Project Dataset, Analytic Sample Formation and Outcome Variables
sec.p: Wisconsin Sleep Cohort (WSC) data were utilised for this project, with these data provided upon request through the National Sleep Research Resource (Young et al. 2009; Zhang et al. 2018). The WSC is an ongoing, longitudinal study of community adults in Wisconsin. Full details on the WSC design and regulatory oversight are available elsewhere (Young et al. 2009).

Participants within the WSC have completed surveys capturing demographic information, medical and psychiatric health, and sleep characteristics while also undergoing in‐laboratory, nocturnal PSG and a MSLT. The initial dataset provided data from 1546 study visits that included an MSLT. The WSC has been ongoing for nearly four decades, with participants often completing multiple follow‐up visits. For this investigation, we only focused on data from the participant's first study visit that included MSLT data (n = 883, Figure 1). We also removed shift‐working participants from the dataset (n = 831, Figure 1). To enhance the generalisability of findings, we focused our analyses on data from clinical protocol MSLTs, after removing research protocol MSLTs that did not allow for sleep after sleep onset and do not mirror current clinical practice (n = 395; removed = 436, Figure 1). Allowing sleep after sleep onset during the nap opportunities is an important component of the clinical assessment process as this affords evaluation of sleep onset rapid eye movement (REM) periods (i.e., REM sleep within 15 min of falling asleep), which are a diagnostic feature of narcolepsy (American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2023). Additionally, five participants were removed because of the absence of sleep diary data (n = 390), with eight more participants removed because of the absence of a PSG sleep staging file (n = 382, Figure 1). Consistent with the naturalistic nature of the WSC, the MSLT protocol allowed participants to use caffeine and/or smoke between MSLT naps, with documentation for each participant. To more closely mirror current clinical protocols, we used this information to create datasets for each analysis (MSL and nap‐specific) that included only participants that had not used caffeine and/or smoked up to that collection point. This resulted in marginally different samples for the primary, MSLT MSL (n = 301) and supplementary Nap 1 (n = 307) and Nap 2 (n = 305) analyses. The samples for Naps 3 and 4 mirrored the primary, MSLT MSL sample. To assess comparability statistically, we compared the three datasets utilised in this investigation across all variables using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and chi‐squared test of independence for continuous and categorical variables, respectively.

sec.p: As most participants (64.8%) did not have a 5th MSLT nap, we limited our focus of this investigation to the first four naps to maintain methodological consistency and preserve sample size. As such, the primary outcome for this investigation, MSLT MSL, is derived from the sleep latency across the first four naps for all participants. Nap‐specific sleep latency is used as the outcome across secondary analyses.

sec.title: Predictor Variables: Missing Data and Formation of Final Predictor List
sec.p: After reviewing the dataset, we developed an initial predictor set of 70 variables that captured demographics, medical and psychiatric health, habitual sleep, prior night PSG sleep and circadian characteristics. These variables were based on existing scientific literature and theoretical understanding of the MSLT and daytime sleepiness.

We explored missingness across variables in this predictor set. Missingness was rare, with most cases complete across variables. We omitted a variable capturing participant's weekly smoking habits due to a high proportion of missing responses across the variable (> 50% missing), which reduced the predictor set to 69 variables. For participants who had missingness on a day of sleep diary data for nap TST, it was assumed the participant did not nap on that day and nap TST was set to 0 min. Some participants did not have a N3 bout on PSG. For these participants, 0 min was used for N3 median bout duration. For a single participant who did not have a REM bout on PSG, 0 min was used for REM median bout duration and the participant's TST was used for REM latency. Another participant did not have documentation for their caffeine or smoking use at Nap 1 on MSLT, despite documentation across all other naps indicating no use of caffeine or smoking. Given the documentation on other naps, it was assumed the participant did not use caffeine or smoke at Nap 1. Only three remaining variables of the 69 in the predictor set had missing data: percentage of PSG with oxygen below 90% (n = 4), Zung depression score (n = 1) and medication use during the MSLT (n = 1). Imputed values were derived for these missing data using the mice package (v3.16.0) in R Studio (R version 4.4.0).

We subsequently utilised correlational analyses to guide the construction of the final predictor set for input to the RF procedure. A threshold approach evaluated the collinearity between predictors, resulting in a final set of predictors that contained 50 variables. This final set of predictors was used across all RF analyses (Table 1). In the final dataset of analytic predictors, no correlation was ≥ 0.75 or ≤ −0.75.

sec.p: Most variables (n = 37) in the final dataset of predictors were derived directly from the WSC dataset. The remaining 13 predictors were derived by the research team, which were comprised of seven sleep diary (bedtime—variation, waketime—variation, total sleep time—average, TST—variation, nap TST—average, nap TST—variation and nap frequency), two PSG (median bout duration—N3 and number of stage transitions per hour—total) and four circadian (CP, sleep diary midpoint—categorical, alignment: sleep diary midpoint and CP (Lok et al. 2024) and duration: sleep diary waketime to Nap 1) variables. CP was formulated based on established thresholds for a middle‐aged, working sample (Taillard et al. 2004). These variables are described in Table 1.

sec.title: Primary and Secondary Analyses: RF, Multivariable Regression and Backward Elimination Stepwise Regression
sec.p: RF is a supervised, decision tree machine learning approach that can be applied for data classification or regression analyses. RF's bootstrapping aggregation of a large number of decision trees reduces the likelihood of overfitting, which is a known problem for other decision tree techniques (Srivastava et al. 2023). RF is a useful tool for feature selection in medical data analyses (Chen et al. 2020; Srivastava et al. 2023). Hyperparameter tuning is a component of RF optimisation, with the number of trees (ntree) and the number of predictors randomly sampled at each decision tree split (mtry) commonly tuned in RF analyses (Probst et al. 2019). For this process, we iterated through seven different ntree values (500, 750, 1000, 1250, 1500, 1750 and 2000) and applied the function tuneRF to identify an ntree and mtry combination based on the lowest out‐of‐bag error rate. RF models with 5‐fold cross‐validation were then computed using these parameters. Predictor importance was determined based on the percentage increase in mean squared error (PIMSE) statistic from the RF model. PIMSE quantifies the increase in mean squared error when a variable is being permuted (i.e., values randomly shuffled). As such, higher values indicate greater importance of a variable for prediction accuracy. This process was performed independently for primary analyses that focused on MSLT MSL as well as secondary analyses that focused on nap‐specific sleep latency (Naps 1, 2, 3 and 4).

The top 10 variables with the highest PIMSE from the RF analyses were selected to undergo further evaluation in regression analyses for both primary and supplementary analyses. A multivariable regression including all 10 variables along with a backwards elimination stepwise regression was performed after removing outliers using Grubbs' test. Akaike information criterion determined variable inclusion/exclusion in the final model for the backwards elimination stepwise regressions.
As an analytic sensitivity check for our primary analyses (i.e., MSLT MSL), results from the RF determined top predictors were compared against results from a forward selection stepwise regression.

RF, multivariable regressions and backwards elimination stepwise regressions were performed in R Studio Statistical Software (v4.4.0; R Core Team 2024). RF analyses used the caret (v6.094), MASS (v.7.3.60.2) and randomForest (v4.7‐1.1) packages.

sec.title: Post Hoc Analyses: Circadian Preference, Nap Number and Their Interaction
sec.p: Post hoc analyses were conducted to evaluate the influence of CP on MSLT MSL. Univariate regression assessed the linear relationship of CP, with CP modelled as a continuous variable from 1 to 3 (morning = 1, neither = 2, evening = 3). Complimentary ANOVA evaluated the main effect of CP as a categorical variable, with subsequent pairwise comparisons performed to assess differences between groups, when appropriate. We also used ANOVA and pairwise comparisons to explore whether the timing of Nap 1 from the MSLT varied based on CP. Additional post hoc analyses were performed that used a mixed effects model that included an interaction term between CP and MSLT nap number to evaluate changes in the relationship between CP and sleep latency across MSLT naps. We also explored whether sleep latency varied significantly across naps using mixed effects models.

Regression and ANOVA analyses were performed in R Studio Statistical Software, with lme4 (v1.1‐35.3) used for mixed effects analyses. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation, unless indicated differently.

sec.title: Sample Demographics and Characteristics
sec.p: The sample demographics and characteristics reflect the primary dataset (Table 1) and include the 50 predictors used in the RF analyses along with additional variables to aid in describing the dataset (Table 1). The demographics and characteristics in datasets used for secondary analyses were either identical to the primary dataset (Naps 3 and 4) or nearly identical to the primary dataset (Naps 1 and 2). No statistical differences were observed when comparing the primary, Nap 1 and Nap 2 datasets, with statistical comparisons resulting in p values ≥ 0.90 across variables.

The primary sample included 301 middle‐aged adults (57.5 ± 7.71 years). The sample was predominantly non‐Hispanic White (percent non‐Hispanic White = 97.0%) with a balanced distribution of males (48.2%) and females (51.8%). Data were collected from 2001 to 2009, with most of the data being collected between 2002 and 2004 (75.8% of data). Average MSLT MSL was 11.9 ± 4.44 min, with 23.3% of the sample demonstrating clinically significant objective daytime sleepiness based on MSLT MSL ≤ 8 min. Average Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) score was 8.91 ± 4.34, with 36.9% of the sample exceeding the ESS threshold (ESS ≥ 11) suggestive of clinically significant subjective daytime sleepiness. Based on sleep diaries, the sample's bedtime was 22:44, risetime was 06:30, and nightly total sleep time was 7.73 ± 0.89 h. The sample averaged a nap on 21.2% of days, with napping time being 34.1 ± 42.9 min. During PSG, the sample had 6.38 ± 0.92 h for TST, 13.4 ± 15.0 min for SOL, 69 ± 36.4 min for WASO and a SE of 81.0% ± 9.05%. AHI was 12.3 ± 17.0 events/h, with 25.9% of the sample displaying moderate or severe sleep apnea (AHI ≥ 15). CP based on Horne–Östberg categories (Taillard et al. 2004) was 46.2% morning, 37.5% neither and 16.3% evening preference.

sec.title: Primary Analyses: MSLT MSL
sec.p: The final model from our primary RF analysis (ntree = 1500; mtry = 24) of MSLT MSL explained 12% of the variance (R 2 = 0.12) (Table S1). Among the top 10 predictors from the RF (Figure 2), PSG SOL emerged as the most important predictor (PIMSE = 26.6%), followed by CP (PIMSE = 8.61%), caffeine use—daily (PIMSE = 8.20%) and ESS score (PIMSE = 7.14%) (Figure 2). In the multivariable regression that included the top 10 predictors from RF, statistical significance was observed for PSG SOL, CP, caffeine use—daily and ESS, whereas the final model from the backward elimination stepwise regression retained these four predictors along with overall health—self‐report (Table 2).

sec.p: In the analytic sensitivity analyses that employed forward selection stepwise regression across all 50 predictors, PSG SOL, CP, caffeine use—daily and ESS emerged as the top four predictors based on ordering in the selection process (Table S2).

sec.title: Secondary Analyses: Nap‐Specific Sleep Latency
sec.p: The final RF models for Nap 1 (ntree = 750; mtry = 11), Nap 2 (ntree = 750; mtry = 16), Nap 3 (ntree = 1000; mtry = 24) and Nap 4 (ntree = 1250; mtry = 24) sleep latency analyses explained 9%, 3%, 7% and 8% of the total variance, respectively (Table S1). Generally, the predictors that emerged as the top 10 most important from RF analyses varied across naps, with variation also seen in the magnitude of importance for top predictors across naps (i.e., PIMSE). PSG SOL displayed the most consistency as a top predictor, ranking either as the top or second predictor across all naps. PSG SOL was the top predictor in RF analyses for Nap 1 (PIMSE = 4.38%), Nap 2 (PIMSE = 6.12%) and Nap 4 (PIMSE = 23.6%) and ranked as the second most important predictor in Nap 3. Caffeine use—daily (PIMSE = 9.38%) was the top predictor in RF analyses for Nap 3. Variable importance plots of the top 10 RF predictors are provided in Supporting Information for Nap 1 (Figure S1), Nap 2 (Figure S2), Nap 3 (Figure S3) and Nap 4 (Figure S4).

In the multivariable regression that included the top 10 predictors from RF for Nap 1, statistical significance was observed for PSG AHI and ESS score, whereas the final model from the backwards elimination stepwise regression included these two predictors along with CP, PSG TST and PSG: number of total stage transitions per hour (Table S3). For Nap 2, statistical significance was observed for ESS score, whereas the final model from the backwards elimination stepwise regression also included PSG SOL, caffeine use—daily, duration between sleep diary average waketime and Nap 1 start time, PSG TST, CP and sex (Table S4). For Nap 3, statistical significance was observed for caffeine use—daily, ESS score, anxiety—state, and sleep diary average variation in waketime, whereas the final model from the backwards elimination stepwise regression also included PSG SOL (Table S5). For Nap 4, statistical significance was observed for PSG SOL, duration between sleep diary average waketime and Nap 1 start time, and sleep diary average total sleep time, whereas the final model from the backwards elimination stepwise regression also included anxiety—trait and CP (Table S6). A compilation of the top predictors across all analyses and their rank ordering based on RF results is presented in Table S7.

sec.title: Post Hoc Analyses: CP and Nap Number
sec.p: MSLT MSL for morning, neither and evening CP groups were 12.7 ± 4.19, 11.4 ± 4.73 and 10.9 ± 4.73 min, respectively (Figure 3). A significant linear relationship between CP and MSLT MSL was observed (β = −0.98, SE = 0.35, 95% CI = [−1.66, −0.3], p = 0.005), suggesting that MSL gets shorter by 0.98 min across each level of CP (morning ➔ neither ➔ evening). A main effect of CP on MSLT MSL was observed (F (2,298) = 4.2, p = 0.02), along with significant pairwise contrasts for morning versus neither (β = −1.27, SE = 0.56, 95% CI = [−2.37, −0.17], p = 0.02) and morning versus evening (β = −1.80, SE = 0.73, 95% CI = [−3.23, −0.36], p = 0.02), but not neither versus evening (Figure 3). CP was also associated with a significant effect on the start time of Nap 1 (F (2,298) = 3.6, p = 0.03). Relative to the morning group, Nap 1 start time was significantly later for the neither group (β = 0.16, SE = 0.06, 95% CI = [0.04, 0.29], p = 0.01), with a statistical trend WWtowards a later start time observed in the evening group (β = 0.14, SE = 0.08, 95% CI = [−0.03, 0.30], p < 0.1) (Figure S5).

caption.p: Multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) mean sleep latency (MSL) across circadian preference groups derived from Horne–Östberg Morningness–Eveningness questionnaire (morning, neither, evening). Group means and standard deviations are plotted, along with participant data points. p values from significant pairwise comparisons between groups are provided.

sec.p: Sleep latencies for Nap 1, Nap 2, Nap 3 and Nap 4 were 12.3 ± 6.09, 11.7 ± 5.89, 11.5 ± 5.64 and 12.2 ± 5.95 min, respectively. Trend‐level significance was observed when evaluating differences in sleep latency across MSLT naps (F (3,900) = 2.44, p = 0.06). Exploratory pairwise comparisons were performed, with significant differences in sleep latency observed for Nap 1 versus Nap 3 (β = −0.81, SE = 0.36, 95% CI = [−1.52, −0.09], p = 0.03) and Nap 3 versus Nap 4 (β = 0.77, SE = 0.36, 95% CI = [0.06, 1.49], p = 0.03).
No significant interaction between CP and nap number on sleep latency was observed when fitting a mixed effects model with CP, nap number and their interaction.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This investigation leveraged RF, machine learning methodology across a high‐dimensional predictor dataset in a large, community sample to advance the understanding of factors that predict MSL from the MSLT. The primary results identified PSG SOL, CP, daily caffeine use and ESS score as the most important predictors of MSLT MSL among those assessed. Specifically, shorter PSG SOL, increased daily caffeine use and higher ESS were associated with shorter MSLT MSL, whereas morning preference was associated with longer MSLT MSL. That said, our large, relatively comprehensive set of 50 predictors relevant to the MSLT and daytime sleepiness showed limited overall explanatory power for MSLT MSL (R 2 = 0.12). The secondary analyses revealed variation in top predictors of sleep latency across MSLT naps; yet, they also provided consistent evidence of PSG SOL as a top predictor for sleep latency across the MSLT. Post hoc analyses provided further support for the association between longer MSLT MSL and morning preference, relative to neither and evening preferences. Overall, the results from this investigation highlight the complex nature of the MSLT, suggest PSG SOL as a uniquely though minorly important predictor of sleep latency on the MSLT and underscore the importance of accounting for circadian characteristics when performing the MSLT while also reflecting the complexity of tailoring the MSLT schedule in practice.

In the primary RF analyses for this investigation, our high‐dimensional set of predictors across demographic, medical and psychiatric, habitual sleep, PSG sleep and circadian characteristics only explained a small proportion of the total variance in MSLT MSL (R 2 = 0.12), with small effects observed from individual predictors. It is possible that other variables absent from our analytic dataset could be better predictors of MSLT MSL, increasing the explanatory value of the overall model. However, these results may simply reflect the complexity and variability of the MSLT. Additionally, a similar investigation by Lok and Zeitzer (2021) that centred on the ESS (i.e., subjective sleepiness) also evidenced low explained variance from their machine learning models using a high dimensional dataset (Lok and Zeitzer 2021). As such, our findings are in alignment with their investigation, perhaps reflecting the complexity of measuring daytime sleepiness, broadly.

PSG SOL emerged as a top predictor of MSLT MSL among those in our dataset, with a positive relationship observed between variables. This is not surprising, given that both variables measure similar metrics (i.e., duration to fall asleep) in the same environment (i.e., in‐laboratory), with primary differences related to time of measurement (nighttime vs. daytime). However, it is unclear to what degree these metrics specifically reflect an individual's level of sleepiness. It seems logical that sleep latency metrics would be tightly connected to one's level of sleepiness. Yet, sleepiness is not necessary, nor sufficient for sleep initiation. ‘Sleepability’ is a term that has been previously used to reflect one's ability to initiate sleep on command or at will (Gupta et al. 2021; Harrison and Horne 1996; Trotti 2016), which seemingly is influenced by an interaction between homeostatic, circadian, psychological and environmental factors, as well as other individual characteristics. Research has shown that some people can display high ‘sleepability’ without sleepiness (Gupta et al. 2021; Harrison and Horne 1996), as well as low ‘sleepability’ (e.g., prolonged SOL) with high sleepiness (Goel et al. 2014). These findings seemingly reflect how other trait‐ and state‐level characteristics can influence the relationship between sleepiness and ‘sleepability’ (Bonnet and Arand 2000). As such, the observed positive relationship between PSG SOL and MSLT MSL may ultimately reflect the shared measurement of ‘sleepability’, which is a characteristic that appears influenced but not fully explained by sleepiness.

It is also important to note that the significant, positive relationship between PSG SOL and MSLT MSL observed in this study aligns with some but not all the existing literature (Chervin et al. 1995; Kayumov et al. 2000). This also pertains to the observed significant, negative relationship between ESS and MSLT MSL (Benbadis et al. 1999; Kelly et al. 2022). For example, a recently performed systematic review and meta‐analysis by Iskander et al. (2023) did not find statistically significant relationships between MSLT MSL and PSG SOL or ESS (Iskander et al. 2023). It is possible that differences in sample characteristics being analysed (e.g., clinical vs. non‐clinical samples; prevalence of daytime sleepiness) contribute to the inconsistent relationships observed across studies.

Other methodological differences between studies (e.g., univariate vs. multivariable analyses; time restricted vs. ad libitum PSG) could also have contributed to the variation in findings. Ultimately, the inconsistency across studies may simply reflect measurement shortcomings. Poor reliability of the MSLT outside of narcolepsy type 1 is well‐established (Lopez et al. 2017; Ruoff et al. 2018; Trotti et al. 2013), with general reliability concerns also attributed to the ESS (Rozgonyi et al. 2021; Scharf 2022) as well as characteristics from PSG due largely to the potential of first night effects (Byun et al. 2019; Ding et al. 2022). These measurement shortcomings may underlie the observed inconsistencies in relationships between MSLT, MSL, PSG SOL and ESS.

Our results also suggest a significant influence of CP on MSLT MSL. A combination of analyses associated the longest MSLT MSL with morning and the shortest MSLT MSL with evening preference while neither preference fell in between. Guidelines from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) note that the timing of a patient's MSLT is important due to the potential impact of circadian phase on MSLT outcomes (Krahn et al. 2021). The guideline recommends tailoring the PSG/MSLT clinical assessment to an individual's sleep–wake schedule. It is noteworthy that the magnitude of difference between CP group levels was 1.27 min for morning versus neither preferences and 1.80 min for morning versus evening preferences. As such, the statistically significant circadian effect may be clinically relevant primarily when patients demonstrate borderline MSLT results (e.g., MSL 8–10 min). Nevertheless, these results do provide further support for the recommendations from the AASM regarding tailoring MSLT timing to a patient's circadian phase. That said, this can be difficult to implement in clinical practice due to logistical constraints (e.g., staff scheduling; patient‐related factors). These constraints may also translate to the research domain, even when the protocols attempt to tailor assessment timing around the participant's preference. For example, the WSC Study manual of operations indicates that the PSG protocol is structured around the participant's preferred bedtime and risetime, which should also influence the timing of the MSLT naps. Due to an absence of data, we were unable to assess whether PSG times varied based on CP. Though we did observe delays in the start time for the MSLT for neither and evening groups, relative to the morning group. However, the delays were relatively modest, with the average for both groups being ~10 min later than the morning group. Overall, these findings add to the small body of evidence highlighting the influence of circadian characteristics on MSLT outcomes while also highlighting the complexity of translating the MSLT protocol into practice.

Despite a rigorous approach applying machine learning techniques, there are potential limitations of our investigation meritorious of discussion. Although the WSC Study provided access to a rich, robust dataset of variables that afforded characterisation across demographic, medical and psychiatric, habitual sleep, PSG sleep and circadian characteristics, our predictor selection was limited to the information collected in this study. It is possible that variables absent from the dataset (and, thus, our RF analyses) could play a larger role in predicting sleep latency on the MSLT than those included in the analyses, which could lead to increased explanatory value of the RF models and alter the variable importance rankings. The characteristics of the sample also limit the generalisability and translation of the findings. Fundamentally, as the investigation was performed in a community‐based sample, these results may not generalise to clinical patients undergoing MSLT. Additionally, the sample was predominantly non‐Hispanic White, which limits the generalisability of these findings to other racial and ethnic groups. Also, the analyses centered on a sample of middle‐aged adults, which may limit translation of findings to other age demographics, including adolescents and older adults. Future research is warranted to better understand the most important predictors of the MSLT for different age groups and across racial and ethnic groups. Additionally, habitual sleep characteristics were derived from a single week of sleep diary data without information on which day of the week corresponded to the provided data. As such, we were unable to compute weighted sleep diary averages that accounted for differences in weekday and weekend characteristics. The inherent subjectivity of sleep diaries also exists as a limitation, with future research striving for objective measures of habitual sleep (e.g., actigraphy) when possible. The absence of actigraphy also limited our circadian characterisation, as we had to rely upon subjective data, questionnaires and sleep diary. At last, the naturalistic design of the WSC protocol afforded participants the ability to use medication on the day of MSLT, yet the available dataset did not provide information on the type of medication utilised. As such, a predictor variable used in RF analyses accounted for general medication use during the MSLT (i.e., yes vs. no), but this variable could not be further subcategorised by medication class. We also included additional predictor variables to reflect self‐reported regular medication use for antihistamines, depression, anxiety, oestrogen, progesterone, sedatives, stimulants and thyroid distinctly, yet it could not be determined whether these were present during MSLT. Given this, it is possible that medication‐specific effects influenced the results of the investigation, as psychotropic medications can confound the interpretation of MSLT results and are frequently encountered in clinical practice (Cairns et al. 2018; Krahn et al. 2021). Future studies that more extensively control for medication use or analyse unmedicated datasets are likely to be a fruitful area of investigation.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In summary, this investigation applied RF, an advanced machine learning technique, on a high‐dimensional dataset from a large, community sample to advance the understanding of factors that predict MSLT MSL. In our primary analyses, our high‐dimensional dataset of 50 predictors that captured demographic, medical and psychiatric, habitual sleep, PSG sleep and circadian characteristics only explained a small portion of the MSLT MSL variance (R 2 = 0.12). This finding seemingly reflects the complex nature of the MSLT and perhaps the assessment of daytime sleepiness, generally. Among the assessed predictors, PSG SOL, CP, daily caffeine use and ESS emerged as the most important predictors of MSLT MSL, with PSG SOL seemingly emerging as the most important of the top predictors. It is possible that the relationship between PSG SOL and MSLT SOL may reflect the shared measurement of ‘sleepability’, a characteristic that is influenced but not fully explained by the degree of sleepiness. Our post hoc analyses underscore the potential impact of CP on MSLT MSL and provide support for AASM recommendations to tailor the assessment to an individual's circadian characteristics. Ultimately, our findings suggest a need for tools and strategies to objectively measure daytime sleepiness that are less susceptible to bias from interindividual differences in circadian characteristics, given logistical challenges to customising the MSLT schedule in clinical practice.

caption.p: Figure S1. Variable importance plot of the top 10 predictors from the random forest analyses for Nap 1 sleep latency of the MSLT. The top 10 predictors are presented on the y‐axis and include sleep onset latency from polysomnography (PSG: SOL), circadian preference, apnea‐hypopnea index from polysomnography (PSG: AHI), total sleep time from polysomnography (PSG: TST), age at collection, Epworth Sleepiness Scale score, average total sleep time from sleep diary (SD: TST—average), wake after sleep onset from polysomnography (PSG: WASO), total number of transitions between sleep stages per hour from polysomnography (PSG: number of stage transitions per hour—total) and percentage of NREM Stage 2 sleep from polysomnography (PSG: N2—Percent). Values reflect percentage increase mean squared error for a given predictor from the random forest, with higher values indicating greater variable importance.

The top 10 predictors are presented on the y‐axis and include sleep onset latency from polysomnography (PSG: SOL), Epworth Sleepiness Scale score, wake after sleep onset from polysomnography (PSG: WASO), caffeine use—daily, variation in nap‐specific total sleep time from sleep diary (SD: nap TST—variation), duration of time (hours) between the sleep diary average waketime and start time of MSLT Nap 1 (duration: SD waketime to Nap 1), total sleep time from polysomnography (PSG: TST), age at collection, circadian preference and sex. Figure S3. Variable importance plot of the top 10 predictors from the random forest analyses for Nap 3 sleep latency of the MSLT.
